question: A September 2024 special report1 by the European Court of Auditors (ECA) has found that the contribution of ‘green’ spending under the EUR 700 billion Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is ‘unclear’ and possibly ‘overestimated’, with some projects having minimal impact on the energy transition or even causing environmental harm. In light of this, the following questions arise: 1.

Does the Commission recognise the risk of an overestimation of up to EUR 34.5 billion in reported climate contributions under the RRF, as identified by the ECA, and what specific actions will the Commission take to ensure that claims of green spending accurately reflect actual expenditures?

What measures will the Commission implement to improve the accuracy and transparency of climate project assessments, prevent misclassifications and address discrepancies between reported and actual impacts?

Does the Commission acknowledge the risk of deliberate misuse of funds under the RRF through intentional misclassification of projects as ‘green’ to meet climate spending targets, and what steps will the Commission take to detect, prevent and hold accountable those responsible for any intentional misreporting?

European Court of Auditors, ‘Special report 14/2024: Green transition – Unclear contribution from the Recovery and Resilience Facility’, 14 September 2024, https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications/SR-202414.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.11.

2024) As specified in the Commission’s reply to the Special Report 14/2024 of the European Court of Auditors’ (ECA)1, the Commission applies, in its calculations of the climate contribution of the national recovery and resilience plans (RRPs), the methodology and specific coefficients that were established by the Parliament and Council in the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation.

Annex VI of the RRF Regulation provides a list of intervention fields with specific climate coefficients2. Since the ECA has not detected any error or misclassification in the Commission’s calculations, the ECA’s conclusion of ‘likely overestimations’ of EUR 34.
5 billion is thus the mathematical consequence of the ECA using a different methodology and different climate coefficients than those set in the RRF Regulation by the co-legislators.

The Commission has invested substantial resources into developing and proposing a sound methodology under RRF to track and report on climate spending in the EU budget, as adopted by the Parliament and the Council, and it considers that the methodology provided in the RRF Regulation and applied by the Commission led to a sufficient level of accuracy.

The Commission is also pursuing opportunities to improve its climate mainstreaming methodology and takes note of all relevant information, including audit findings. The Commission ensures a high degree of transparency about the climate contribution of national RRPs, for instance by publishing the RRF Annual Reports and by regularly updating the Recovery and Resilience Scoreboard.
